Northrop's cost estimate for the B-2 development contract increased by $6.8 billion between February 1987 and January 1991, to a total of $18 billion.
The estimate for the low-rate initial production contract increased by about $0.5 billion over the original contract price during a similar time period.
Aircraft numbers 1 and 2 were assembled in about 4.6 million production labor hours, exceeding the combined goal of about 3.3 million hours by 40%.
Aircraft numbers 3 and 4 are projected to require about 3.6 million production labor hours, about 30% higher than the combined goal of 2.8 million hours.
The number of manufacturing defects decreased on each successive aircraft, but was larger than anticipated.
Defect rates, as a percentage of production labor hours, improved for Northrop in 1990 compared to 1989, but increased at Boeing.
A total of 122,700 changes were made to engineering drawings through August 1990, including 29,500 in 1988 and over 22,000 in 1989 and 1990.
The planned hours of work transferred to final assembly increased from 3,712 hours for aircraft 3 in 1988 to 7,153 hours in 1991, a 93% increase.
Northrop estimated the 7,153 hours of transferred work for aircraft 3 would require about 401,000 actual production labor hours to complete.
Schedule changes between February 1987 and December 1990 provided 11 to 24 months of additional time for the contractors to complete work on the major sections before shipment to final assembly.
In April 1990, the Secretary of Defense reduced the quantity of B-2s to be purchased from 132 to 75 aircraft due to total costs and changing world conditions.
The revised cost estimate for the 75 aircraft program was $63.7 billion as of January 1991.
The President's FY1992 and FY1993 budget requests 4 aircraft and $4.8 billion in FY1992, and 7 aircraft and $4.6 billion in FY1993.
Northrop submitted a corrective action plan for tool proving in May 1990, which was accepted. As of March 1991, Northrop was about 15% complete, LTV was 63% complete, and Boeing was 92% complete.
The B-2 combines conventional and state-of-the-art aircraft technology, including special shaping and use of radar-absorbing materials to reduce the radar cross-section for stealth requirements.
